intro.text: Week 8 — Architecture, SOLID Principles & Design Patterns
Comprehensive study notes; expanded code examples and additional exercises are explicitly supplementary teaching material.

Read the “why” before memorizing the definition. For each pattern or principle, identify the original design problem, the proposed structure, and its trade-off. Sketch the relationships from memory and answer the checks at the end.
1. Software architecture: styles, components, connectors and design smells
2. SOLID principles: S, O, L, I, D
3. Creational patterns: Factory Method and Builder
5. Behavioral patterns: Iterator, Observer and Strategy
6. Pattern selection, common confusions and exam revision

blocks.text: Software architecture is a way of organising your code: how classes/modules should be organised. It is like the architecture of a building, considering efficiency of space and functionality. It defines the software elements/modules, the relations among them, and the properties of both. This is the “big picture view” taken after design — modular/layered design and UML.
1.1 Why architecture matters
Reflect on Google search versus a compiler. Their components interact differently.
These patterns of information between components are called software architecture styles.
1.2 Client–server
In client–server architecture, data is transacted in response to requests.
Google search: the query goes to a server, which returns a response; this is predominantly how the Internet works.
1.3 Pipe-and-filter
Data is passed from component to component and transformed/filtered along the way.
Compiler: source code → assembly code → executable file run by the OS.
1.4 Model–View–Controller (MVC)

MVC separates views of the data from manipulations of the data. Model = the component that models the data for the service. In the Amazon Seller portal, these are the classes/objects that model the database tables.

View = GUI objects, the presentation layer and visual representation of the model; it retrieves data from the model and displays it. Controller = coordinates multiple views on the screen and helps users manipulate the model, e.g. filtering catalogue items by name.
1.5 Peer-to-peer
Peer-to-peer is a distributed application where systems form nodes and share resources. There is no centralised system monitoring all transactions.
Nodes make processing power, disk storage etc. directly available to other nodes without central coordination.
1.6 Components, connectors and protocols

Component = well-defined functionality or behaviour, separate from other functionality, e.g. client software and server; browser and search-engine server. Connectors = code that transmits information between components and regulates their interaction.
Protocol = a set of predefined rules describing how components interact; client and server must agree on the message format. The most common connectors are function calls and REST API calls.
1.7 Design patterns, design smells and refactoring

blocks.caption: Design Patterns, Design Smells and Refactoring
blocks.alt: Design Patterns, Design Smells and Refactoring

blocks.text: Past solutions that experienced designers reused became standardised. A design pattern is a description of communicating objects and classes customised to solve a general design problem in a particular context. An anti-pattern is a pattern used incorrectly, or new code added along the way.

Design smells are warning signs that your code may be heading towards an anti-pattern. SOLID guidelines help avoid design smells. Refactoring moves back to a good design: moving code between classes, creating new classes/modules, and removing classes that are not required.
Summary
Styles: client-server, pipe and filter, peer-to-peer, MVC.
Design patterns: common patterns of organising code that have worked in the past.
Design smell: lack of proper design patterns.

sections.title: SOLID: five principles for maintainable object-oriented design

blocks.text: SOLID is a set of object-oriented principles for software design, conceptualised by Robert Martin (“Uncle Bob”), one of the founders of the Agile Manifesto. They make code easy to understand and modular, and support good cohesion and loose coupling. S = Single Responsibility, O = Open–Closed, L = Liskov Substitution, I = Interface Segregation, D = Dependency Inversion.
2.1 S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

Every class should have a single responsibility/purpose. The original Seller class held seller ID, name, address and product, and had addSeller, deleteSeller, addProduct, and add/delete/view inventory.

Split it into Seller (seller details, addSeller, deleteSeller), Product, and Inventory (takes seller ID; products are added to the seller’s inventory). This lets Product change without major changes to Seller/Inventory, and makes mistakes easier to find because the code is isolated.
2.2 O — Open–Closed Principle (OCP)

Software entities should be open for extension, closed for modification: extend behaviour, e.g. through subclasses, without modifying existing classes. Product has ID, name, type and cost. Adding size/colour and a new addProduct to Product violates OCP.
Instead, create Clothing extending Product with size and colour. A Book subclass with author and publisher is added the same way.
2.3 L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)

LSP applies to inheritance hierarchies. “Derived classes should be substitutable by their base class”: if D is a subtype of B, we can replace B with D without interrupting the behaviour of the program. The feature is to notify sellers about feedback on their product by email.

Abstract class FeedbackNotification has abstract notify(product, feedback, email); EmailNotification extends it. Adding SMSNotification breaks this: it needs a mobile number, not an email, so the derived method cannot substitute the base one.

Fix: remove email from the abstract notify(product, feedback). EmailNotification takes email in its constructor; SMSNotification takes mobile number and carrier in its constructor. Both implement notify(product, feedback).

blocks.caption: The Substitution Problem: Email vs SMS
blocks.alt: The Substitution Problem: Email vs SMS

blocks.text: 2.4 I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)

An interface is a group of related methods with empty bodies; it specifies what, not how. Other classes implement it by implementing all its methods. Interface Segregation: “do not force any client to implement an interface which is irrelevant to them”. DeliveryProcessing defines placeOrder(), notifySeller(), packageOrder(), deliver(). An online/e-book order does not need packaging or delivery to an address, so the last two methods are irrelevant to it.

Split it into PhysicalDeliveryProcessing (placeOrder, notifySeller, packageOrder, deliver) and OnlineDeliveryProcessing (placeOrder, notifySeller, provideDownloadLink(Product p, String url)). Each client implements only the interface it needs.
2.5 D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

Prefer abstractions/interfaces over implementations; always associate classes with interfaces rather than actual implementations. A seller should receive payment for products sold. Seller has a BankAccount attribute with number, branch and balance. Adding Paytm, Google Pay or UPI would mean adding more attributes, so Seller is tightly coupled and the code gets complex.

Fix: interface PaymentAccount with payment(); BankAccount, UPI, GooglePay and Paytm implement it; Seller is coupled to PaymentAccount. In main, create the chosen payment object (e.g. BankAccount, later UPI) and pass it to the seller.

blocks.caption: Every New Payment Option Changes Seller
blocks.alt: Every New Payment Option Changes Seller

blocks.text: 2.6 How the principles differ

SRP asks whether a class has a cohesive job. OCP asks how expected new behavior can be added. LSP asks whether a subtype honors its parent contract. ISP asks whether a client is forced to use irrelevant methods. DIP asks whether important business logic depends on a concrete detail instead of a stable abstraction.

rows: One class changes for unrelated reasons
Adding a product type means editing the existing Product class
Subclass cannot substitute the base method (e.g. notify needs email)
Client must implement irrelevant methods (e-book: packageOrder, deliver)
Business code creates a specific provider

blocks.text: Follow these principles to make code more efficient, maintainable and easy to understand; they recur in design patterns.

Design patterns are descriptions of communicating objects and classes customised to solve a general design problem in a particular context. Elements: Problem — when and in what context to apply it; Solution — elements, relationships, responsibilities and collaborations, a template for many situations; Consequences — results, trade-offs and cost-benefit. Types: Creational — used during object creation; Structural — composition of classes/objects; Behavioural — how classes/objects interact and distribute responsibility.
3.1 Factory Method: choose what to create

Feature: deliver a package using a courier service. Delivery has deliver(courier), and Courier is a class. Adding international couriers with a courierType if/else in deliver violates OCP. Factory pattern: replace direct object construction calls (the new operator) with calls to a special factory method.

Make Delivery and Courier abstract. NationalCourier and InternationalCourier extend Courier. NationalDelivery and InternationalDelivery extend Delivery and implement createCourier(), returning NationalCourier / InternationalCourier. In main, create a delivery object d (e.g. InternationalDelivery), call d.createCourier(), and pass the result to d.deliver(). New types, e.g. a local courier, are just new classes.
Pros: SRP and OCP. Con: code may become more complicated because of many new subclasses, so decide based on context.
3.2 Builder: construct a complicated object step by step

Book has mandatory ISBN, title and cost, and optional author, published and description. Many constructors for different combinations are telescoping constructors. Builder extracts object construction out of its own class into a separate builder object.

A static Builder class has the same fields, a Builder(isbn, title, cost) constructor, one method per optional field — author(), published(), description() — and build() returning the Book. Book keeps one constructor that takes the builder. Example: new Book.Builder(isbn, title, cost).author(..).published(..).description(..).build().

Pros: construct objects step by step; SRP. Con: more complicated because of the new class and methods; skip it if there are not many optional parameters. The example is adapted from Joshua Bloch’s builder (Oracle Java Magazine).
3.3 Factory Method versus Builder
Factory Method: courier creation — which object to create? Builder: Book construction — how to build the object step by step?
Structural patterns help assemble objects and classes into larger structures while keeping them flexible and efficient.
4.1 Facade: one simple entry point to a complex workflow

Problem: you must create several objects and perform several steps in the right order with the right parameters, using existing complicated library functions. Anyone reusing your code must know all of this. After a buyer places an order: create order, notify seller, prepare packaging, send for delivery — classes Order, Seller, Package, Delivery.
Facade provides a simple interface to a library or complex set of classes: DeliveryFacade.deliver(...) creates the objects and calls them in order; the client calls only deliver.

Pro: isolates code from other libraries’ and classes’ complexity. Con: the facade is tightly coupled to other objects, so maintenance is harder; any change in Order/Seller/Package/Delivery needs a change in DeliveryFacade.
4.2 Adapter: connect incompatible interfaces

Problem: some products cost dollars/euros and must be converted to rupees, but Product cannot directly use the existing ConversionCalculator library because its interface is incompatible and not under our control. The client calls the adapter’s method; the adapter calls the adaptee’s method, wrapping the object and hiding the incompatibility.
CostCalculatorAdapter takes a product, creates a ConversionCalculator and passes the cost. Product creates the adapter and gets the cost in rupees (example: $300).

Pros: SRP — conversion code is separated from Product’s business logic; OCP — new adapters for other currencies. Con: overall code complexity increases, and it is unnecessary if you could change Product or access ConversionCalculator directly.
4.3 Facade versus Adapter
Facade gives a simple interface to many classes; Adapter makes incompatible interfaces work together.
Behavioural patterns handle effective communication and the assignment of responsibilities between objects.
5.1 Iterator: traverse a collection without exposing storage

Collections include lists, queues, stacks and trees of products, orders or deliveries. The client only wants to access elements, not know how they are stored. Separate element access into an iterator object. Java’s Iterator interface has hasNext(), returning true if there are more elements, and next(), returning the next element.
Example: Book (ISBN, title, cost) in an ArrayList and in a LinkedList. Each collection implements hasNext/next and the client just iterates.
Pros: SRP; OCP through new iterator types. Con: overkill for simple collections such as arrays.
5.2 Observer: notify interested subscribers automatically

Feature: notify a particular set of buyers when a new product launches, like YouTube channel subscriptions — only subscribers, not all users. Subject keeps a list of observers and notifies them automatically of changes.
Subject provides register(), unregister(), notifyObservers(); notifyObservers() iterates and calls update().
Observer is an interface/abstract class with update(). NormalUser and PrimeUser implement update(); a prime user also gets an extra-discount message.
5.3 Strategy: select an interchangeable algorithm

blocks.caption: Strategy Pattern — FIFOOrderDelivery is the shortened label for FirstInFirstOutOrderDelivery.

blocks.text: Feature: process orders by different strategies — first in first out, or priority (prime users first). Before: OrderManager has one method per strategy; adding a strategy means modifying the class, violating OCP. Strategy extracts each algorithm into its own class; the context delegates to a strategy object.
Interface OrderDeliveryStrategy defines deliverOrders(). FirstInFirstOutOrderDelivery and PriorityOrderDelivery implement it; a new strategy is just a new class.
Pros: isolates algorithm implementation; OCP. Con: not required if only one or two algorithms will be used.
5.4 Observer versus Strategy versus Iterator

Observer broadcasts changes to subscribers. Strategy swaps the algorithm used to perform a task. Iterator moves through elements of a collection. All three are behavioral, but the reasons for using them are different.
Summary

Patterns are templates/descriptions for organising objects and classes to solve general design problems in a context. There are about 23 patterns; the course covers a few. Weigh their benefits and drawbacks: patterns should not be used blindly, only when they give a benefit.

When choosing a design approach, first identify the problem described in the sections: overall system organization (architecture), class responsibilities and dependencies (SOLID), object creation (creational patterns), interface compatibility or subsystem simplification (structural patterns), or object communication and algorithm selection (behavioral patterns). The comparison below summarizes these distinctions.

Large Seller class mixes unrelated tasks

blocks.text: Question 1
A class manages seller details, inventory and sales reports. Which principle is at risk?
Answer and reasoning: SRP: the class has multiple reasons to change. Split seller, inventory and reporting responsibilities.
Question 2
A new payment provider requires editing Seller.processPayment(). Which principle suggests a redesign?
Answer and reasoning: DIP: Seller should depend on a payment abstraction. OCP also explains why extensibility is desirable.
Question 3
An e-book processor must provide an empty deliver() method. Why is that a problem?
Answer and reasoning: ISP: its interface includes a method irrelevant to the digital-order client.
Question 4
A subclass has the same method signature but throws an error for inputs accepted by its base class. Is LSP satisfied?
Answer and reasoning: No. Substitutability requires honoring the behavioral expectations of the base type.
Question 5
A client needs one operation to create an order, notify the seller and dispatch a parcel. Which pattern?
Answer and reasoning: Facade: it provides one simplified entry point to multiple subsystem steps.
Question 6
A product priced in dollars must get its cost in rupees from an existing ConversionCalculator it cannot call directly. Which pattern?
Answer and reasoning: Adapter (CostCalculatorAdapter): wraps the existing conversion library’s incompatible interface.
Question 7
A Book has mandatory ISBN, title and cost and optional author, published year and description. Which creational pattern?
Answer and reasoning: Builder: construct it step by step instead of using many telescoping constructors.
Question 8
Buyers should automatically learn about newly launched products. Which pattern?
Answer and reasoning: Observer: register buyers and notify them on a launch event.
Question 9
An order queue can be processed FIFO or by customer priority. Which pattern?
Answer and reasoning: Strategy: encapsulate the alternative algorithms behind a shared interface.
Question 10
You need to iterate over a tree without revealing its internal node representation. Which pattern?
Answer and reasoning: Iterator: separate traversal from collection representation.

I can distinguish client–server, pipe-and-filter, MVC and peer-to-peer.
I can identify the problem, refactoring and trade-off for each SOLID principle.
I can explain why e-book orders should not implement packageOrder() and deliver() (split into Physical/OnlineDeliveryProcessing).
I can distinguish Factory Method from Builder and Facade from Adapter.
I can identify Iterator, Observer and Strategy from an unfamiliar scenario.
I can explain at least one advantage and one cost of introducing each pattern.
